questions.question: Practical station on Candida krusei.

parts.text: Given the broth microdilution, read the minimum inhibitory concentration.
How would you report the susceptibilities?

parts_raw.text: Given broth microdilution. Read MIC.
How would you report susceptibilities?

questions.model_answer: a) [image-based question: read the MIC as the lowest antifungal concentration in the broth microdilution series showing no visible growth.] b) Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole: report it as resistant to fluconazole regardless of the measured MIC. Report susceptibility to voriconazole, echinocandins, and amphotericin B, applying species-specific CLSI breakpoints/epidemiologic cutoff values.
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI antifungal breakpoints / IDSA candidiasis guidance: C. krusei is inherently fluconazole-resistant.

questions.question: An 800 g infant with necrotizing enterocolitis on fluconazole prophylaxis and a PICC line develops Candida albicans bloodstream infection.
questions.question_raw: 800g infant with NEC on fluconazole prophylaxis and PICC line; develops Candida albicans BSI.

parts.text: What is the drug of choice per IDSA guidelines?
Give three reasons according to the IDSA guidelines why this is preferred.
What other intervention must be done?

parts_raw.text: What is the drug of choice per IDSA guidelines?
Give three reasons according to the IDSA guidelines why this is preferred.
What other intervention must be done?

questions.model_answer: a) Amphotericin B deoxycholate. b) (1) There is the most clinical experience with this agent in neonates. (2) The infant developed breakthrough infection on fluconazole prophylaxis, so a non-azole agent is preferred because of possible azole resistance/failure. (3) It achieves good penetration into the CNS and urinary tract, important because neonatal candidiasis frequently disseminates (including to the CNS). c) Remove the central venous (PICC) catheter; also perform a lumbar puncture and dilated retinal examination given the risk of disseminated/CNS disease.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2016 candidiasis guideline, neonatal candidiasis section.

cohort_answer.text: Drug of choice: Amphotericin B deoxycholate. Reasons: Most experience in this age group; Patient has been on fluconazole ppx so might be resistant; Well tolerated in this age group; Reaches CNS/urine well. Other intervention: A lumbar puncture and a dilated retinal examination are recommended in neonates with cultures positive for Candida species from blood and/or urine; Removal of CVC; CT or ultrasound imaging of the genitourinary tract, liver, and spleen should be performed if blood cultures are persistently positive for Candida species

questions.question: A hemodynamically stable person who injects drugs has Candida endocarditis; transesophageal echocardiography confirms infective endocarditis.
questions.question_raw: Candida endocarditis in hemodynamically stable IVDU. TEE shows IE.

parts.text: Name two empiric therapies.
Name two management steps other than antifungals or surgery/echocardiography.
Give four indications for surgery in infective endocarditis (other than fungal etiology).

parts_raw.text: Name two empiric therapy.
Management other than antifungals or surgery/echo – name two.
Four indications for surgery in IE (other than fungal).

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Liposomal amphotericin B, with or without flucytosine. (2) High-dose echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin). b) (1) Remove the central venous catheter and repeat blood cultures to document clearance. (2) Dilated retinal (ophthalmologic) examination for ocular involvement. c) (1) Heart failure due to valve dysfunction (severe regurgitation/obstruction). (2) Uncontrolled infection — persistent bacteremia or fever despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy. (3) Perivalvular extension — abscess, fistula, or new heart block/conduction abnormality. (4) Prevention of embolism — large (>10 mm) mobile vegetation, especially with recurrent emboli on therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2016 candidiasis guideline (Candida endocarditis); AHA/ESC infective endocarditis surgical indications.

cohort_answer.text: Empiric therapy: Liposomal Ampho B +/- flucytosine or high dose echinocandin. Other management: Dilated retinal exam; Repeat blood culture to document clearance; Removal of CVC. Four indications for surgery in IE: not documented

questions.question: A farmer presents ill with fever, arthritis, and a maculopapular rash, including a 1x2 mm non-blanchable lesion. Two weeks earlier, while working in a grain bin, he had acute pain in the hand with puncture wounds. Gram stain of the wound shows spiral-shaped gram-negative bacilli.
questions.question_raw:
Q62 (2008)
Farmer presents sick with fever, arthritis, maculopapular rash. 1x2mm non-blanchable rash. 2 weeks ago working in grain bin, acute pain in hand with puncture wounds. Gram stain of wound shows spiral shaped GNB.

parts.text: What are two organisms that can do this?

parts_raw.text: B) What are 2 organisms that can do this?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Streptobacillus moniliformis; (2) Spirillum minus. Both cause rat-bite fever, consistent with rodent exposure in a grain bin, fever, arthritis, and rash.

questions.question_raw: Farmer presents sick with fever, arthritis, macular-papular rash. 1x2mm non-blanching rash. Two weeks ago was working in grain bin, acute pain in hand with puncture wounds. Gram stain of wound shows spiral shaped bacilli

parts.text: What is the diagnosis?
What are two organisms that can do this?
What are two treatment options?

parts_raw.text: What is the diagnosis?
What are 2 organisms that can do this?
What are 2 treatment options

questions.model_answer: a) Rat-bite fever. b) (1) Streptobacillus moniliformis; (2) Spirillum minus (predominant in Asia). c) (1) Intravenous penicillin G (drug of choice); (2) Ceftriaxone (or oral tetracycline/doxycycline for penicillin-allergic patients). Also clean the wound and give tetanus prophylaxis if warranted.

cohort_answer.text: Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat bite fever) - non-motile spiral GNB, transmitted from rodents via bite/scratch/ingestion, found in North America. Two organisms: Streptobacillus moniliformis, Spirillum minus (found mostly in Asia). Treatment: Penicillin G 2 million q4h x10-14d (alternative doxy or ceftriaxone); wound care; tetanus immunization; consider prophylactic 3 day course of clavulin for rat bites

questions.question: Give the Gram stain, catalase (if relevant), and confirmatory test for Streptococcus agalactiae, Proteus vulgaris, Candida albicans, and Enterococcus.
questions.question_raw:
Q66 (2013 AM, 2015)
What is the gram, catalase (if relevant), confirmatory test for: Strep agalactiae, Proteus vulgaris, Candida albicans, Enterococcus

parts.text: Give the Gram stain, catalase, and confirmatory test for each organism.

parts_raw.text: Give gram stain, catalase, and confirmatory test for each organism

questions.model_answer:
Streptococcus agalactiae: gram-positive cocci, catalase negative, Lancefield group B antigen (also CAMP/hippurate positive).
Proteus vulgaris: gram-negative bacilli, catalase positive, oxidase negative, swarming/urease positive, indole positive (distinguishes from P. mirabilis).
Candida albicans: gram-positive yeast, germ-tube positive (and chlamydospore formation).
Enterococcus: gram-positive cocci in pairs/short chains, catalase negative, PYR positive with bile-esculin hydrolysis and growth in 6.5% NaCl; reacts with Lancefield group D antisera.
questions.beyond_mandell: Identification data for S. agalactiae, Proteus vulgaris, and Candida albicans are from standard clinical microbiology (Murray Manual of Clinical Microbiology); this chapter covers only the Enterococcus tests.

cohort_answer.text:
GPC, cat neg, Lancefield antigen test
GNB, cat pos, índole pos, ornithine decarboxylase neg (mirabilis - pos)
Gram pos, cat pos, germ tube positive (dublinensis is the only other pos germ tube)
GPC, weakly pos/ usually cat neg, bile eschulin hydrolysis (grows well in 6.5% NaCl)

questions.question: A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia and a central venous catheter has blood cultures growing yeast that are germ-tube negative.
questions.question_raw: A patient with ALL and a CVC. Blood cultures grow yeast that are germ tube negative.

parts.text: What two different antifungal agents could you start empirically, and give their mechanisms of action?
List two things to follow up on in addition to starting antifungals.

parts_raw.text: What 2 different antifungal agents could you start empirically (and give mechanisms of action)?
List 2 things to follow-up with in addition to starting antifungals.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) An echinocandin (e.g., caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin) — inhibits beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, blocking synthesis of an essential fungal cell-wall polymer. (2) Liposomal amphotericin B — binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that cause leakage of cell contents and cell death. (Germ-tube negativity indicates a non-albicans species; empiric echinocandin covers likely fluconazole-resistant species such as C. krusei/C. glabrata.) b) (1) Remove the central venous catheter and repeat blood cultures every 24-48 h to document clearance. (2) Obtain a dilated ophthalmologic (fundoscopic) examination for endophthalmitis once the neutrophil count recovers, and send species identification with antifungal susceptibility testing.
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA 2016 candidiasis guideline: echinocandin first-line for candidemia in neutropenic patients; catheter removal, follow-up cultures, and ophthalmologic exam recommended.

cohort_answer.text: Echinocandin – inhibits beta 1,3 D-glucan synthase; Amphotericin B – inhibits ergosterol synthesis which is important to maintain cell wall integrity. (C. krusei – fluconazole resistant, voriconazole/isavuconazole sensitive.) || Removal of CVC, repeat blood culture 24-48 hours after initiating antifungals; Eye exam when neutrophils recover.

questions.question: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole.
questions.question_raw: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole

parts.text: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole.

parts_raw.text: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole

questions.model_answer: Candida resists fluconazole by several mechanisms, often in combination: (1) Overexpression/upregulation of ERG11 (the target, lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase), increasing enzyme levels so the drug cannot fully suppress ergosterol synthesis. (2) Point mutations in ERG11 altering the azole-binding site so fluconazole binds poorly. (3) Upregulation of efflux pumps — ATP-binding cassette transporters (CDR1/CDR2) and major facilitator superfamily pumps (MDR1) — that reduce intracellular drug concentration. (4) Bypass/loss-of-function mutations in ERG3, preventing accumulation of the toxic 14-alpha-methyl sterol that normally results from azole blockade.

questions.question: Give the Gram stain, colony morphology, catalase (if applicable) and rapid bench identification test and result for the following organisms.
questions.question_raw: 21. Give Gram stain, colony morphology, catalase (if applicable) and rapid bench ID test and result for: a) Group B Strep; b) Enterococcus spp.; c) Candida albicans; d) Proteus vulgaris

parts.text: Group B Streptococcus
Enterococcus species
Candida albicans
Proteus vulgaris

parts_raw.text: a) Group B Strep
b) Enterococcus spp.
c) Candida albicans
d) Proteus vulgaris

questions.model_answer:
a) Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae): Gram-positive cocci in chains; grey-white colonies with a narrow zone of beta-haemolysis on blood agar; catalase negative; rapid test - Lancefield group B latex agglutination positive (CAMP test positive, hippurate hydrolysis positive; bacitracin resistant).
b) Enterococcus species: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains; small grey non-haemolytic (alpha or gamma) colonies; catalase negative (may be weakly/pseudo-positive); rapid test - PYR positive and bile-esculin positive with growth in 6.5% NaCl (LAP positive).
c) Candida albicans: budding yeast, stains Gram-positive; white creamy pasty colonies, may show 'feet' (marginal hyphal fringe) on cornmeal/agar; catalase not applicable; rapid test - germ tube positive in serum at 3 h (also C. dubliniensis), with terminal chlamydospores and pseudohyphae on cornmeal-Tween 80.
d) Proteus vulgaris: Gram-negative bacilli; swarming waves of growth over blood agar, lactose non-fermenter, produces H2S; catalase positive, oxidase negative; rapid test - urease positive (rapid) and indole positive (distinguishing it from indole-negative P. mirabilis); ornithine decarboxylase negative (positive in P. mirabilis).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort called Enterococcus 'catalase weak positive'; enterococci are catalase negative (a weak pseudocatalase reaction may be seen on blood-containing media).

cohort_answer.text:
GBS – GPC chains, catalase negative, beta hemolytic, lancefield group B
Enterococcus – GPC pairs/chains, catalase weak positive, alpha or gamma hemolytic, PYR + (GAS too), LAP, bile esculin positive
Candida albicans – "Gram positive" yeast, feet on morphology, germ tube + (also dublinesis), pseudohyphae on wet mount (also with glabrata)
Proteus vulgaris – GNB, catalase +, swarming colony, indole positive, OTC neg (mirabilis +), urease +

questions.question_raw: You are seeing a patient with a pet rat. He likes to play with his rat and gets lots of scratches. He presents now with fever, chills, and fatigue. He has a blood culture return showing a pleomorphic, gram-negative, filamentous rod.

parts.text: What is the syndrome, and two organisms that cause this syndrome (genus and species)?
What single antibiotic can you use to treat it?
What are two viruses you could acquire from rat excrement in Canada (specifically in Canada, so not Hantaan or Lassa fever)?

parts_raw.text: What is the syndrome and TWO organisms that cause this syndrome (genus AND species please)
What antibiotic (only 1) can you use to treat?
What are TWO viruses that you could get from rat excrement IN CANADA (specifically said in Canada so no Hantaan or Lassa fever for you)

questions.model_answer: a) Syndrome: rat-bite fever. Organisms: (1) Streptobacillus moniliformis; (2) Spirillum minus. b) Penicillin G (intravenous). c) (1) Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV); (2) Seoul virus (a hantavirus present in North America). Both are acquired from rodent excreta/secretions in Canada.
questions.beyond_mandell: Rodent-associated viruses in Canada (LCMV, Seoul hantavirus) are from PHAC/CDC zoonoses sources, not this chapter.

questions.question: Name the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.
questions.question_raw: What are the typical organisms infecting in the following scenarios.

parts.text: Cochlear implants.
Laceration that occurs in a lake.
Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash.
A person competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high liver enzymes, and conjunctival suffusion.

parts_raw.text: Cochlear implants.
Laceration that occurs in a lake
Rat bite in a child who now has fever and rash
Guy competing in a triathlon in South America has fever, high LFTs and conjunctival suffusion

questions.model_answer: a) Streptococcus pneumoniae (leading cause of cochlear implant-associated meningitis; also Haemophilus influenzae). b) Aeromonas hydrophila (also Pseudomonas aeruginosa; freshwater exposure). c) Streptobacillus moniliformis (rat-bite fever; Spirillum minus in Asia). d) Leptospira species (leptospirosis) — fever, elevated LFTs, and conjunctival suffusion after freshwater exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rat-bite (part c) organism is from this chapter; cochlear implant, freshwater laceration, and leptospirosis organisms are from established Mandell/IDSA knowledge in other chapters.

cohort_answer.text: Cochlear implants: meningitis most commonly S. pneumoniae, less often H. influenzae; localized wound infection most commonly S. aureus (also CoNS, streptococci, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Achromobacter xylosoxidans, Candida albicans); mastoiditis most commonly S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus, Pseudomonas spp, H. influenzae. Lake laceration (fresh/brackish water): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Aeromonas hydrophila, Chromobacterium violaceum (immunosuppression/CGD), Mycobacterium fortuitum, Plesiomonas shigelloides, Edwardsiella tarda, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Streptococcus iniae (fish preparation); salt water: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (fish preparation), Mycobacterium marinum, Shewanella spp, Vibrio vulnificus. Rat bite: Streptobacillus moniliformis (most US cases); Spirillum minus (Asia). Triathlon South America: Leptospirosis - abrupt fever, rigors, myalgias, headache after incubation 2-26 days (average 10); conjunctival suffusion important but often overlooked sign (~55% of patients), uncommon in other diseases; subconjunctival hemorrhages also occur.
